meta.title: Who really said "Never attempt to win by force what can be won by deception"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Machiavelli never wrote it. Wikiquote lists the line as misattributed to The Prince; its documented ancestor is a 1982 Commentary essay paraphrasing him.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Never attempt to win by force what can be won by deception'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Machiavelli. The sentence is absent from The Prince and the Discourses - it traces to a 1982 paraphrase in Commentary magazine.

answer.label: Not Machiavelli’s words — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The sentence appears nowhere in Machiavelli. Wikiquote ↗ files it under “Misattributed,” noting that it is falsely credited to The Prince and is “not found there textually,” and the writer Ian Chadwick, who searched more than seventeen translations of Machiavelli, traces the line ↗ to a 1982 magazine paraphrase by the journalist Edward Jay Epstein — who told him by email that it may have been just that, a paraphrase.

source.heading: What Machiavelli actually wrote

docMeta.dd: None of Machiavelli’s works — not The Prince, not the Discourses, not the Art of War
Edward Jay Epstein, “Disinformation,” Commentary, July 1982 (paraphrase, wording “by fraud”)
Excerpt below: Ninian Hill Thomson, 1883 (Kegan Paul, Trench & Co., London)

source.excerpt: I hold it as most certain that men seldom if ever rise to great place from small beginnings without using fraud or force, unless, indeed, they be given, or take by inheritance the place to which some other has already come. Force, however, will never suffice by itself to effect this end, while fraud often will, as any one may plainly see who reads the lives of Philip of Macedon, Agathocles of Sicily, and many others like them, who from the lowest or, at any rate, from very low beginnings, rose either to sovereignty or to the highest command.
trail: Wikiquote’s Machiavelli page ↗ carries the line in its Misattributed section, with the note that it is “falsely attributed to The Prince, which is not found there textually.”

Ian Chadwick, who runs a long-standing Machiavelli site and owns more than seventeen translations of the works, reports that “Machiavelli never wrote those words” ↗ and traces the saying to a 1982 article on disinformation by Edward Jay Epstein.

That article is “Disinformation: Or, Why the CIA Cannot Verify an Arms-Control Agreement,” Commentary, July 1982 ↗, where Epstein puts a Machiavelli maxim about force and fraud in quotation marks without citing a source for it.
We read the standard public-domain English texts end to end: the phrase is in neither W. K. Marriott’s The Prince ↗ — where the word deception does not occur at all — nor Thomson’s Discourses ↗.
source.cutTag: Discourses on Livy, Bk. II, ch. 13
source.excerptNote: This is the closest Machiavelli gets — the opening of Discourses on Livy, Book II, chapter 13, whose title Thomson renders “That Men rise from humble to high Fortunes rather by Fraud than by Force.” Note what it is: an observation about how men climb, not the crisp tactical order the internet puts in his mouth.

sourceLink.text: Discourses on the First Decade of Titus Livius, trans. Ninian Hill Thomson (1883), Project Gutenberg

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the popular one-liner, because no author has been identified for that exact wording. The excerpt displayed above is Ninian Hill Thomson’s 1883 translation of the Discourses, long in the public domain; the 1982 Commentary essay that carries the earlier “by fraud” paraphrase is a modern work and remains in copyright.

author.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
author.kicker: The thought is his. The sentence is not.
author.heading: About Machiavelli
author.bio: Niccolò Machiavelli served as secretary to the second chancery of the Republic of Florence from 1498 until the Medici restoration of 1512 swept him out of office, and he wrote The Prince in exile the following year. He is the most quoted and least read political writer in the Western canon, which is precisely why he is such a magnet for invented maxims: anything cold-eyed and tactical sounds like him. His actual argument about deceit is longer, more hedged and more interesting than the one-liners pinned to his name — in the Discourses he praises fraud in war and in the climb to power, while insisting it is never glorious to break a promise you actually gave.

cite.sourceCitation: No source in Machiavelli. The line’s documented ancestor is Edward Jay Epstein, “Disinformation: Or, Why the CIA Cannot Verify an Arms-Control Agreement,” Commentary, July 1982, which paraphrases Machiavelli on force and fraud without citing any source; the popular “deception” wording is a later variant. Compare Niccolò Machiavelli, Discourses on the First Decade of Titus Livius, trans. Ninian Hill Thomson (London: Kegan Paul, Trench & Co., 1883), Bk. II, ch. 13 and Bk. III, ch. 40.

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: Three separate things get muddled here: the book it is stamped on, the words themselves, and the idea underneath them. Only the idea belongs to Machiavelli.

items.why: Quote sites and social posts routinely tag the line “— Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince.” Wikiquote ↗ lists it under Misattributed precisely because it is not found there textually — and the word deception does not occur anywhere in W. K. Marriott’s standard English translation ↗.

Writing about Soviet deception of US intelligence, Epstein said Machiavelli strongly recommended that a ruler should ‘never attempt to win by force what he might otherwise win by fraud’ — inside quotation marks, with no citation attached. Read the essay ↗. Ian Chadwick, who asked him about it, reports that Epstein suggested it may have been a paraphrase ↗.

The line is often blurred with “All warfare is based on deception,” a genuinely separate sentence that Epstein quoted a few paragraphs further into the same 1982 essay ↗. Sun Tzu and Machiavelli end up sharing a caption that belongs to neither.

misattribution.truthLine: Machiavelli really did argue that fraud beats force — Book II, chapter 13 of the Discourses ↗ is titled “That Men rise from humble to high Fortunes rather by Fraud than by Force.” What people quote is a twentieth-century summary of him, not a translation of him.

context.heading: Why this one sticks
lead: The reason this fake works is that it is not wrong about Machiavelli — it is just not by him. He devoted a whole chapter of the Discourses to the proposition that men climb “rather by Fraud than by Force,” and another, Book III chapter 40, titled in Thomson’s translation “That Fraud is fair in War,” which opens: “Although in all other affairs it be hateful to use fraud, in the operations of war it is praiseworthy and glorious.” A reader who has absorbed that will nod along to the one-liner without pausing, which is exactly how paraphrase hardens into quotation.

What seems to have happened is ordinary and slightly banal. In July 1982 Edward Jay Epstein opened a Commentary essay on Soviet disinformation by summarising Machiavelli’s force-or-fraud argument, and set his summary inside quotation marks. Quotation marks are the load-bearing error: once a paraphrase is punctuated as a quotation, every later hand copies it as one. Somewhere in the reposting the plainer, harder-hitting word deception displaced fraud, and the sentence lost its last tie to anything Epstein had read.
detailsBody: The chapter people cite is The Prince, chapter 18, “Concerning the way in which princes should keep faith” — the fox-and-lion chapter. It is genuinely about deceit, and it is genuinely ruthless: “a wise lord cannot, nor ought he to, keep faith when such observance may be turned against him.” But nothing in it reads like the quoted maxim, and Marriott’s translation does not contain the word deception anywhere.

A full-text search of book databases turns up no printing of either wording before the 1982 essay, and the “deception” variant does not surface in books until the 2010s — which is consistent with an internet-era mutation rather than a lost translation. Treat that as a floor, not a proof: absence from a search index is weaker evidence than the direct textual check, which is why the textual check is what this page rests on.

There is one more strand worth separating out. Epstein’s essay also quotes Sun Tzu’s “All warfare is based on deception” a few paragraphs later, and the two lines have been travelling together ever since. They are different sentences by different people, and only one of them is real.
